items.good: From the opening under the name alone, the reader gets the idea the tool rests on (sorting by extension into six fixed kind folders under a built-in rule that no file is deleted, renamed or overwritten), the kind of thing it is (a terminal command on macOS and Linux), whom it is for (anyone whose Downloads folder is too full to find a file in) and what they gain (finding a file by opening the one folder of its kind, with every file still there), so they can tell whether it is for them.

The reader follows one use on a Downloads-like test folder they make themselves, in the order it happens: they make the folder, preview, move, see what the folder now holds, change one file by hand, preview the undo and undo, with the exact output the tool gives back at each step and what the folder ends up as, so they picture using it on their own Downloads folder from start to result.

Each item of Why sets one thing only this tool gives against a named other way (sorting by hand in a file manager, a sort-by-type view, a script of mv commands, rule-based sorting apps): a preview the move run then matches, a way back from the last run, no overwrite where mv would replace a file, and no setup; no benefit every way gives is listed.

parts.good: The reader takes in the opening at once: each kind folder is named where 'kind folder' is first used, and the rule is said in full.

Each command is in a block to copy and each output in a block of its own; 'left', 'kind not known' and 'subfolder' are explained right after the first output that shows them, the default folder and the folder as last word are said before the first command that uses it, the Linux path is given where /Users/me first appears, and why images/ and documents/ are removed is said right before the run that removes them.
Each item reads alone as one sentence naming the other way it is set against, with its explanation under it; 'the rule' points back to the opening, read before.
Each requirement is said as what it is; pipx, the one a newcomer may not know, is said in a few words with a working link to how to install it, and Git with why it is needed.
Install, first use on the real Downloads folder and removal are each a block to copy, in the order the reader does them, with the Example linked as the way to try it first.
The reader learns what fuller use docs/ux.md holds (the full kind table, every reason, where the record is kept) and that there is no change history yet, without following the link first.
A builder reads in one sentence where how the tool is built and tested is written.
The reader reads the license by name, the MIT License, as the user decided.

items.good: Each sentence says a thing once: the opening holds the idea and the gain, Why holds only the contrasts with other ways, the Example alone walks the commands and outputs, Installation points to the Example for trying it rather than repeating it, and the full kind table and every reason are left to docs/ux.md; there is no part for a reviewer and no history of decisions.

questions.question: The README's Development section, which the readme checklist's template asks for as a link to the entrance to the architecture and development, links to docs/architecture.md, which the plan's task T3 makes and which is not in the repository yet. Keep that link, the file to be added by T3 as the CCS's LICENSE decision does for LICENSE, or name another entrance?
questions.recommended: Keep the link to docs/architecture.md and add it to this call's CCS as a decision that T3 adds that file, as the plan already makes it there and it is where a builder looks for how the tool is built and tested.

chosen.chosen: The Example uses a test folder ~/test-downloads made with mkdir and touch, holding report.pdf, photo.JPG, setup.crdownload and a projects/ subfolder, and moves photo.JPG into projects/ by hand before the undo.
chosen.why: AC8 asks that the user can run the tool on a test Downloads folder of their own making; the files come from docs/ux.md's own examples, and the hand move shows a 'not moved back' case with the same summary wording docs/ux.md gives ('Moved back 1 file. 1 file not moved back.'), as docs/ux.md does not say how a count of 0 is printed.

chosen.chosen: Install by git clone https://github.com/lovaizu/playground.git, cd playground, pipx install .
chosen.why: AC1 installs from this repository with pipx install .; the URL is the repository of the pull request in steering.md, checked with git ls-remote.

chosen.chosen: Remove with pipx uninstall organize-downloads, the package named as the command.
chosen.why: AC1 says pipx uninstall removes it but names no package; naming the package as the command lets the reader remove it without looking the name up, and the build must name the package so.

chosen.chosen: Documentation says the tool has had no release yet, so no changes between versions are written, and links docs/ux.md for fuller use.
chosen.why: The template asks where what changed in each version is written; no such file exists and nothing has been released, and docs/ux.md holds the full kind table and every reason.

chosen.chosen: The License section names the MIT License without linking the LICENSE file.
chosen.why: The decision says the README names it and the LICENSE file is still to be added; a link would point at a file not there yet.

chosen.chosen: The Why section sets the tool against sorting by hand in a file manager, a sort-by-type view, a script of mv commands and rule-based sorting apps.
chosen.why: The template asks for the other ways of doing the same work, which no file of the CCS names; these are the ways a terminal user would otherwise sort a Downloads folder.
